unit.name: Biology: Life on Earth and Ecosystems
unit.subtitle: Producers, food webs and the case for protecting biodiversity.

lessons.title: Photosynthesis and Plant Growth
lessons.description: How producers turn light into chemical energy, and what limits the rate.
lessons.content_html:
Producers and the Flow of Energy

All food chains begin with a producer. Green plants and algae are producers because they capture light energy and use it to manufacture glucose — a process called photosynthesis. Without producers, no energy would enter the food web and life as we know it could not exist. This makes understanding photosynthesis central to understanding ecosystems.

Photosynthesis is an endothermic reaction: it takes in energy from the surroundings rather than releasing it. The light energy absorbed by the green pigment chlorophyll is converted into chemical energy stored in glucose molecules. This stored energy can then be released by respiration — in the plant itself and in every consumer that feeds on the plant.

Key Fact

Photosynthesis is endothermic and occurs in chloroplasts:
carbon dioxide + water → glucose + oxygen (using light energy)
\(6CO_2 + 6H_2O \rightarrow C_6H_{12}O_6 + 6O_2\)

Inside the Chloroplast

Photosynthesis occurs in chloroplasts, which are found mainly in the mesophyll cells of leaves. Chloroplasts contain stacks of membrane discs called grana, which have a large surface area for capturing light. Chlorophyll molecules embedded in these membranes absorb light — mainly red and blue wavelengths — which is why leaves appear green (green light is reflected, not absorbed).

Photosynthesis can be thought of in two stages. In the first stage, light energy is used to split water molecules, releasing oxygen as a by-product. In the second stage, the hydrogen ions released are used to convert carbon dioxide into glucose. Both stages take place within the chloroplast. The oxygen released enters the atmosphere, making photosynthesis the source of almost all atmospheric oxygen on Earth.

What Happens to Glucose in the Plant?

Once glucose is produced, the plant uses it in several ways:

  • Respiration — glucose is broken down to transfer energy for the plant’s own metabolic processes, such as active transport and protein synthesis.
  • Starch storage — excess glucose is converted to starch, which is insoluble and can be stored without drawing water into cells by osmosis.
  • Cellulose — glucose is polymerised into cellulose for cell wall construction, giving the plant structural support.
  • Amino acids and proteins — by combining glucose with nitrate ions absorbed from the soil, the plant makes amino acids, which are assembled into proteins for growth and enzymes.

Plants absorb mineral ions from the soil through their root hair cells by active transport. Nitrate ions (NO₃⁻) are used to make amino acids and proteins, and hence DNA. A deficiency in nitrate leads to stunted growth and yellowing of leaves because the plant cannot make adequate protein.

Magnesium ions (Mg²⁺) are needed to make chlorophyll. Without sufficient magnesium, chlorophyll production falls and leaves turn pale yellow-green — a condition called chlorosis. In the absence of chlorophyll, photosynthesis is severely limited, reducing the plant’s ability to grow.

Limiting Factors

The rate of photosynthesis is controlled by whichever factor is in shortest supply. A limiting factor is the one variable that, if increased, would allow the rate to rise. When conditions are otherwise ideal, increasing a limiting factor speeds up photosynthesis; when that factor is no longer limiting, a different one takes over.

Three main abiotic factors act as limiting factors: light intensity, carbon dioxide concentration, and temperature. Understanding them allows growers to optimise crop yields — for example, in a commercial greenhouse where all three factors can be controlled.

Light intensity: As light intensity increases, more energy is available for the light-driven stage of photosynthesis, so the rate rises. Eventually the rate plateaus because a different factor (CO₂ or temperature) becomes limiting. Light intensity decreases with the square of the distance from the source: double the distance, quarter the intensity.

Carbon dioxide concentration: CO₂ is a raw material for the second stage of photosynthesis. Increasing CO₂ supplies more substrate for the carbon-fixation reactions, raising the rate. In greenhouses, farmers sometimes add CO₂ gas to boost yields.

Temperature: Photosynthesis is enzyme-controlled. As temperature rises, enzyme and substrate molecules move faster, increasing the collision rate and the reaction rate. Above the optimum temperature, enzymes begin to denature and the rate falls sharply.

Key Fact

Limiting factors for photosynthesis: light intensity, CO₂ concentration, temperature. At the plateau on a rate-vs-light-intensity graph, light is no longer limiting — another factor (CO₂ or temperature) has taken over. Increasing all three together can allow the rate to rise further.

Transpiration and Water Loss

Water taken in through the roots travels up the plant in xylem vessels and eventually evaporates from the leaf surface through tiny pores called stomata. This process — transpiration — drives a continuous column of water up from the roots. Stomata must be open to allow CO₂ in for photosynthesis, but opening them also allows water vapour to escape. Plants balance this trade-off using guard cells, which open and close the stomata in response to conditions such as light and water availability.

At Higher Tier, you need to be able to interpret rate-of-photosynthesis graphs where multiple limiting factors interact. For example, if increasing CO₂ concentration raises the plateau on a rate-vs-light graph, this confirms that CO₂ was previously limiting at that light intensity. If increasing temperature also raises the plateau, temperature was also limiting. Only by holding two factors constant while varying the third can you identify each factor’s individual contribution.
lessons.exam_tip_html: Questions on limiting factors commonly include a graph. Read the axes carefully: the x-axis is usually light intensity, CO₂, or temperature, and the y-axis is rate of photosynthesis. When the line plateaus, identify the new limiting factor. When explaining a plateau, state both what is no longer limiting AND what is now limiting. Avoid vague answers like “there is no more light” — instead write “CO₂ concentration is now the limiting factor, even though light intensity continues to increase.”
lessons.conclusion_html:
Key Takeaways

  • Photosynthesis is an endothermic process in chloroplasts: \(6CO_2 + 6H_2O \rightarrow C_6H_{12}O_6 + 6O_2\). Chlorophyll absorbs light energy to drive the reaction.
  • Glucose is used for respiration, starch storage, cellulose synthesis, and making amino acids (when combined with nitrate ions).
  • Light intensity, CO₂ concentration and temperature are the three main limiting factors; whichever is in shortest supply controls the rate of photosynthesis.

practice_questions.text: Write the word equation and the balanced symbol equation for photosynthesis.
practice_questions.marks:
1 mark: carbon dioxide + water → glucose + oxygen (light energy required, accept above or below the arrow).
1 mark: 6CO₂ + 6H₂O → C₆H₁₂O₆ + 6O₂ (allow light energy notation).

practice_questions.text: A student grows two identical tomato plants. Plant A is grown in a greenhouse with increased CO₂ concentration; Plant B is grown in a greenhouse with normal CO₂ concentration. Both greenhouses have the same temperature and light intensity. Predict and explain the difference in growth rate between the two plants.
practice_questions.marks:
Mastering: Plant A grows faster [1]; CO₂ is a reactant in photosynthesis, so a higher concentration increases the rate of carbon fixation [1]; more glucose is produced per unit time, providing more energy for respiration and more building blocks for growth [1].
Secure: States Plant A grows faster [1]; links to more CO₂ increasing the rate of photosynthesis [1].
Developing: States Plant A grows faster without a clear explanation.
Emerging: Identifies CO₂ without linking to growth.

practice_questions.text: Explain the effect of temperature on the rate of photosynthesis, including what happens above the optimum temperature.
practice_questions.marks:
Mastering: As temperature increases, enzyme and substrate molecules have more kinetic energy and collide more frequently, increasing the rate [1]; above the optimum, the enzyme’s active site changes shape (denatures) permanently [1]; substrate can no longer bind, so the rate falls sharply [1].
Secure: Temperature increases rate up to optimum [1]; above optimum enzymes denature [1].
Developing: States rate increases with temperature, then falls.
Emerging: States temperature affects rate.

practice_questions.text: A gardener notices that her tomato plants have yellow-green leaves and stunted growth. Suggest which mineral ion is deficient and explain how the deficiency causes these symptoms.
practice_questions.marks:
Mastering: Nitrate deficiency causes stunted growth because nitrates are needed to make amino acids and therefore proteins (and DNA) [1][1]; magnesium deficiency causes yellowing (chlorosis) because magnesium is needed to make chlorophyll [1][1]. (Accept either deficiency with full explanation for 4 marks.)
Secure: Correct deficiency identified [1]; mechanism linked to symptom [1].
Developing: Names a deficiency without explaining the mechanism.
Emerging: States a mineral is missing.

practice_questions.text: Describe how a student could use pondweed to investigate the effect of light intensity on the rate of photosynthesis in a school laboratory.
practice_questions.marks:
Mastering: Place pondweed in a beaker of water with the lamp at a measured distance [1]; count oxygen bubbles per minute (or measure gas volume using a gas syringe) [1]; change the distance from the lamp to alter light intensity, keeping temperature and CO₂ concentration constant [1]; repeat each distance at least three times and calculate a mean [1].
Secure: Uses distance to change light intensity [1]; counts bubbles [1]; two further valid points.
Developing: Describes set-up and mentions bubbles, limited method detail.
Emerging: States pondweed is used without methodological detail.

practice_questions.text: Explain why plants store excess glucose as starch rather than keeping it as glucose.
practice_questions.marks: 1 mark: Starch is insoluble, so it does not lower the water potential of the cell (does not cause water to enter by osmosis), making it safe to store in large amounts without affecting cell turgor (accept: starch is compact and insoluble, suitable for storage).

glossary_terms.definition: An organism that makes its own food using an external energy source such as sunlight; green plants and algae are the main producers in most ecosystems.
The process by which plants and algae use light energy to convert carbon dioxide and water into glucose and oxygen, occurring in chloroplasts.
A chemical reaction that takes in energy from the surroundings, such as light energy absorbed during photosynthesis.
The green pigment found inside chloroplasts that absorbs light energy and uses it to drive the reactions of photosynthesis.
A membrane-bound organelle found in plant cells that contains chlorophyll and is the site of photosynthesis.
An insoluble polysaccharide used by plants to store glucose; because it is insoluble, it does not affect the cell's water potential by osmosis.
Charged particles of mineral elements dissolved in water and absorbed by plants through root hair cells for use in growth and metabolic processes.
The factor present in the lowest concentration relative to a plant's needs, preventing the rate of photosynthesis from increasing even if other conditions are favourable.
The permanent change in an enzyme's active site shape due to excessive heat or extreme pH, which prevents the substrate from binding.
Tiny pores mainly on the underside of leaves through which gas exchange and water vapour loss (transpiration) occur.
The evaporation of water from a plant, mainly through the stomata on the leaf surface, driven by the evaporation-cohesion-tension mechanism.

lessons.title: Ecosystems and Interdependence
lessons.description: Food chains, food webs and the niches species depend on. Key concepts and applications explained.
lessons.content_html:
What is an Ecosystem?

An ecosystem consists of all the living organisms in an area together with the non-living environment they inhabit. The living (biological) part is called the community; the non-living part is called the habitat. Ecosystems can range enormously in scale — from a garden pond to an oak woodland to the open ocean — but all share the same fundamental structure: producers capture energy, consumers transfer it, and decomposers recycle it.

The conditions of an ecosystem are shaped by abiotic factors (non-living) and biotic factors (living). Abiotic factors include temperature, rainfall, light intensity, pH, and mineral availability. Biotic factors include competition for food or space, predation, disease, and the availability of mates. Both sets of factors determine which species can survive in a given place and how abundant they become.

Key Fact

Abiotic factors (non-living): temperature, light intensity, rainfall, pH, mineral availability. Biotic factors (living): competition, predation, disease, parasitism. Both shape which species survive and in what numbers.

Food Chains and Food Webs

A food chain shows the linear transfer of energy from one organism to the next. It always begins with a producer — a photosynthetic organism such as a plant or alga — followed by a series of consumers. Each feeding step is called a trophic level. Primary consumers (herbivores) eat producers at trophic level 2; secondary consumers eat primary consumers at trophic level 3, and so on.

In reality, most species eat and are eaten by multiple other species. A food web is a more accurate model of feeding relationships in an ecosystem. For example, in a UK oak woodland, caterpillars may be eaten by blue tits, warblers, or spiders — and blue tits themselves may be eaten by sparrowhawks or cats. Removing or adding any species can have cascading effects throughout the web.

Arrows in a food web point in the direction of energy flow — from the organism being eaten to the organism eating it. Each arrow represents a feeding relationship. To trace energy, follow arrows from producer to apex predator.

When answering questions about what happens when a species is removed, work through the web systematically. If a prey species is removed, its predators lose a food source and may decline; if a predator is removed, its prey may increase — and then the prey’s food source (the next level down) may decrease because it is being over-consumed. These knock-on effects are called trophic cascades.

Ecological Niches and Competition

Every species occupies a niche: its unique role in the ecosystem. The niche includes not just what the organism eats, but where it feeds, when it is active, how it reproduces, and how it interacts with other species. No two species can occupy exactly the same niche in the same ecosystem indefinitely — one will out-compete the other and drive it to local extinction or force it to adapt. This is the competitive exclusion principle.

Competition occurs when two or more organisms require the same limited resource. Intraspecific competition (between individuals of the same species) drives natural selection within species. Interspecific competition (between different species) shapes the composition of communities over time. In UK grasslands, for example, red and grey squirrels compete for hazelnuts — because grey squirrels can digest acorns more efficiently and carry squirrelpox virus without symptoms (which is fatal to reds), they have displaced red squirrels from most of England and Wales.

Key Fact

A niche is the full role of a species in its ecosystem — what it eats, where it lives, and how it interacts with others. No two species can share an identical niche: the more competitive will prevail over the other in the long term.

Interdependence

Interdependence means that species in a community depend on one another. These dependencies include feeding relationships, but also more subtle interactions: plants depend on bees for pollination; bees depend on flowers for nectar; trees depend on mycorrhizal fungi for mineral uptake; fungi benefit from tree sugars in return. These relationships mean that the loss of one species can ripple through an entire community.

A striking example of interdependence is the relationship between predators and their prey. Predator and prey populations often oscillate in linked cycles: when prey is abundant, predator numbers rise; as more predators hunt, prey numbers fall; with less prey, predator numbers also fall; prey then recovers — and the cycle repeats. This oscillation keeps both populations in a dynamic balance, provided no external factors intervene.

Some species form particularly close interdependent relationships called symbioses. In mutualism, both species benefit: clownfish hide among sea anemone tentacles for protection while deterring fish that would eat the anemone. In parasitism, one species (the parasite) benefits at the expense of the host: fleas feed on mammal blood, reducing the host’s fitness without immediately killing it. Parasites are very different from predators — predators kill and consume their prey, while parasites live on or in the host long-term.

Population Size and Carrying Capacity

The maximum population size a habitat can support is called the carrying capacity. When a population reaches the carrying capacity, limiting factors — food shortage, disease, predation, or competition for space — keep it in check. A population that overshoots its carrying capacity will decline as resources are exhausted, and may even crash below it temporarily before recovering.

This framework explains why populations in stable ecosystems rarely undergo extreme booms or crashes. Feedback mechanisms between predators, prey, disease organisms, and resource availability buffer the system, maintaining a dynamic equilibrium. Human activity can disturb this equilibrium — by over-hunting, habitat destruction, or introducing non-native species — pushing populations outside the range that natural feedback can correct.
lessons.exam_tip_html: When a question gives you a food web and asks what happens when a species is removed, trace every arrow connected to that species and predict effects at each trophic level. Use words like “increase,” “decrease,” or “could go either way” and justify each one. For 6-mark questions on interdependence, structure your answer as a logical sequence of effects rather than a list — this demonstrates the reasoning the mark scheme rewards.
lessons.conclusion_html:
Key Takeaways

  • An ecosystem is a community of organisms interacting with each other and the non-living environment; abiotic and biotic factors both shape which species survive and in what numbers.
  • Food webs show interconnected feeding relationships at different trophic levels — removing one species can trigger trophic cascades throughout the web.
  • Every species occupies a unique niche; interdependence means species depend on each other for resources and services, so the loss of one population can affect many others.

practice_questions.text: Explain the difference between an abiotic and a biotic factor. Give one example of each in a UK freshwater pond ecosystem.
practice_questions.marks:
1 mark: abiotic = non-living physical/chemical factor (e.g. water temperature, pH, light intensity, dissolved oxygen).
1 mark: biotic = living component (e.g. predatory fish, competing algae, disease organisms, availability of invertebrate prey).

practice_questions.text: A food web in a UK meadow includes: grass → voles → kestrels; grass → rabbits → foxes; voles → foxes. A disease kills most of the rabbit population. Predict and explain the likely short-term effects on the kestrel and fox populations.
practice_questions.marks:
Mastering: Fox population decreases because rabbits are a major prey source [1]; foxes may then eat more voles as an alternative prey [1]; vole population decreases due to increased fox predation [1]; with fewer voles, kestrel population could decrease [1]; accept alternative valid chain with reasoning; conclusion weighs the net effect on each species [1].
Secure: Correct direction for at least two populations with valid reasons [1][1]; one further valid linked effect.
Developing: Identifies one population change without clear reasoning.
Emerging: States a population changes without linking it to the food web.

practice_questions.text: What is a niche? Explain why two species that occupy identical niches cannot coexist in the same ecosystem long-term.
practice_questions.marks:
Mastering: A niche is the full role of a species in its ecosystem (what it eats, where, when, how it interacts) [1]; two species occupying the same niche compete for identical resources [1]; the more competitive species will out-compete the other, which is displaced or goes locally extinct [1].
Secure: Defines niche [1]; explains competition leads to one species winning [1].
Developing: States they compete without explaining the outcome.
Emerging: States they need the same things.

practice_questions.text: Describe the difference between mutualism and parasitism, giving one example of each.
practice_questions.marks:
Mastering: Mutualism: both species benefit [1]; example e.g. clownfish and sea anemone, or bee pollination of flowers [1]; Parasitism: parasite benefits, host is harmed [1]; example e.g. flea and mammal, or tapeworm in gut [1].
Secure: Correct definition of each with one valid example each.
Developing: One type correctly defined with example.
Emerging: Names one type without definition.

practice_questions.text: Explain what is meant by the carrying capacity of an ecosystem.
practice_questions.marks: 1 mark: The maximum population size that an environment can sustainably support, determined by the availability of resources such as food, water and space.

practice_questions.text: Evaluate the claim that removing a top predator from an ecosystem will always result in an increase in the prey population.
practice_questions.marks:
Mastering: Initial increase in prey likely as predation pressure removed [1]; however, prey may over-consume their own food source (plants/lower consumers), reducing its availability [1]; increased intraspecific competition among prey as numbers grow [1]; disease spread may increase at high density [1]; other predators may fill the vacant niche [1]; balanced conclusion: short-term increase likely, long-term outcome depends on other limiting factors [1].
Secure: Short-term increase explained [1]; at least two qualifying factors identified.
Developing: States prey increases without qualification.
Emerging: Agrees or disagrees with no scientific reasoning.

glossary_terms.definition: A community of living organisms interacting with each other and with the non-living physical environment in a particular area.
The non-living physical and chemical components of an ecosystem, such as temperature, light, water availability, pH and soil type.
The living components of an ecosystem, including all organisms that interact with each other through feeding, competition, predation and disease.
An organism that produces its own food by photosynthesis and forms the starting point of all food chains.
A level in a food chain or food web, defined by the number of energy transfers from the producer; producers are at trophic level 1.
A network of interconnected food chains showing all the feeding relationships among the species in a community.
The role a species plays in its ecosystem, including what it eats, when it is active, where it lives, and how it interacts with other species.
The interaction between organisms requiring the same limited resource, resulting in reduced success for the less competitive individual.
The way in which species in a community rely on each other for resources, services, or survival, so that a change in one population affects others.
A close relationship between two species in which both benefit from the association.
A close relationship between two species in which one benefits (the parasite) and one is harmed (the host).
The maximum population size that an environment can sustainably support, determined by the availability of resources such as food, water and space.

lessons.title: Carbon, Nitrogen and Water Cycles
lessons.description: Tracing the elements that move endlessly through the living world.
lessons.content_html:
Why Elements Must Cycle

Energy flows through ecosystems in one direction: it enters as sunlight, is captured by producers, and is lost as heat at each trophic level. But matter is different. The atoms that make up living organisms — carbon, nitrogen, oxygen, hydrogen — are neither created nor destroyed. They move continuously between living organisms and the non-living environment through biogeochemical cycles. Understanding these cycles explains how the same carbon atom in your body may once have been in a dinosaur, and the same nitrogen atom may have been in the soil last year.

Human activity has altered all three major cycles: burning fossil fuels disrupts the carbon cycle; fertiliser use and sewage release disrupt the nitrogen cycle; urbanisation and deforestation alter the water cycle. Understanding each cycle helps us predict and address these disruptions — an important connection to the chemistry and physics content on climate change.

The Carbon Cycle

Carbon moves between the atmosphere, living organisms, and the Earth’s crust. In the atmosphere, carbon exists mainly as carbon dioxide (CO₂). Producers remove CO₂ from the atmosphere during photosynthesis, incorporating carbon into glucose and other organic molecules. This carbon then passes through food chains as organisms eat one another.

Respiration — all living organisms respire, oxidising glucose and releasing CO₂. This applies to producers, consumers, and decomposers alike.

Decomposition — when organisms die, decomposers (bacteria and fungi) break down organic molecules through their own respiration and enzymatic activity, releasing CO₂. Without decomposers, dead material would accumulate and nutrients would be locked away permanently.

Combustion — burning organic material (wood, fossil fuels, peat) releases CO₂ rapidly. Fossil fuels — coal, oil and natural gas — are ancient organic carbon that was buried before decomposition could occur and has remained locked underground for millions of years. Burning these fuels releases carbon that has been out of the active cycle for vast geological periods, raising atmospheric CO₂ concentrations.

Key Fact

Carbon enters the biotic cycle through photosynthesis (CO₂ → organic molecules). It returns to the atmosphere through respiration (all organisms), decomposition (bacteria and fungi), and combustion (burning of organic material). Burning fossil fuels adds ‘ancient’ carbon to the active cycle, raising atmospheric CO₂.

The Nitrogen Cycle

Nitrogen makes up the majority of the atmosphere as nitrogen gas (N₂), but most organisms cannot use it in this form. The nitrogen cycle describes how nitrogen is converted into usable compounds and then returned to the atmosphere. It depends heavily on specialised bacteria at each key step.

Nitrogen fixation — nitrogen-fixing bacteria convert N₂ gas into ammonia (NH₃) or nitrate ions (NO₃⁻). Some live freely in the soil; others live in root nodules of leguminous plants (peas, beans, clover), forming a mutualistic relationship where the plant provides sugars and the bacteria provide fixed nitrogen.

Nitrification — nitrifying bacteria in the soil convert ammonium ions (from decomposition) first into nitrite ions and then into nitrate ions. Nitrate ions can be absorbed by plant roots via active transport.

Denitrification — denitrifying bacteria operate in waterlogged, anaerobic soils. They convert nitrate ions back into nitrogen gas, which returns to the atmosphere. This is why waterlogged soils are less fertile — denitrification removes available nitrogen faster than nitrification can replace it.

Decomposition — decomposers break down dead organic matter and excretory products, releasing ammonium ions back into the soil. This connects the carbon and nitrogen cycles, because decomposers carry out both processes simultaneously.

Key Fact

The nitrogen cycle relies on bacteria: nitrogen-fixing bacteria (N₂ → NH₃/NO₃⁻), nitrifying bacteria (NH₄⁺ → NO₂⁻ → NO₃⁻), denitrifying bacteria (NO₃⁻ → N₂), and decomposers (organic N → NH₄⁺). Plants absorb nitrate ions from the soil to make amino acids and proteins.

Human Disruption of the Nitrogen Cycle

Farmers add nitrogen to the soil through fertilisers — either as inorganic compounds (manufactured using atmospheric nitrogen through the Haber process) or as organic material (manure, compost). When excess nitrate is washed out of soil by rain, it enters waterways. This process — called eutrophication — triggers algal blooms that block light, causing aquatic plants to die. Decomposers feeding on the dead material consume oxygen, leaving the water depleted of dissolved oxygen and causing the death of fish and other aerobic organisms.

The Water Cycle

Water moves continuously between the oceans, atmosphere, land and living organisms. The main driving force is solar energy, which causes evaporation from water surfaces. When water vapour cools at altitude, it condenses into clouds. Precipitation (rain, snow, hail) returns water to the land, where it soaks into the ground (infiltration), flows as surface run-off into rivers and eventually the ocean, or is taken up by plants.

Organisms play an active role in the water cycle. Plants absorb water through their roots and release it as water vapour through their stomata — a process called transpiration. Forests return large amounts of water to the atmosphere through transpiration; deforestation therefore reduces local atmospheric moisture and can alter rainfall patterns. This links the water cycle to climate change — warmer temperatures increase evaporation rates and alter precipitation globally.

Urbanisation replaces permeable soil and vegetation with impermeable concrete and tarmac. This reduces infiltration and increases surface run-off, raising the risk of flash flooding after heavy rainfall. At the same time, less water soaks into groundwater reserves, reducing the natural replenishment of aquifers — an important freshwater resource.

Deforestation removes trees that would otherwise intercept rainfall and return it to the atmosphere through transpiration. The result is increased run-off, soil erosion, and a drier local climate. These effects are particularly significant in tropical regions where forests generate much of their own rainfall through the water vapour they release.
lessons.exam_tip_html: Questions on the nitrogen cycle often test the names and roles of specific bacteria. Learn them as a sequence: nitrogen fixation (N₂ → usable forms) → decomposition (organic N → NH₄⁺) → nitrification (NH₄⁺ → NO₃⁻) → plant uptake → back into organisms → death → decomposition again. Denitrification (NO₃⁻ → N₂) is a ‘leak’ from the cycle under anaerobic conditions. For 5- or 6-mark questions, always explain the mechanism rather than just naming the process.
lessons.conclusion_html:
Key Takeaways

  • Carbon cycles between the atmosphere and organisms via photosynthesis (in), respiration (out), decomposition (out), and combustion (out); burning fossil fuels adds ancient carbon to the active cycle.
  • The nitrogen cycle depends on four types of bacteria: nitrogen-fixing, nitrifying, denitrifying, and decomposing. Plants absorb nitrate ions from the soil to make amino acids and proteins.
  • The water cycle is driven by solar energy (evaporation) and gravity (precipitation, run-off). Human activities such as deforestation and urbanisation disrupt this cycle, affecting local climate and flood risk.

lessons.title: Evolution by Natural Selection
lessons.description: Darwin, Wallace and the mechanism that links every living thing.
lessons.content_html:
The Problem Darwin and Wallace Set Out to Solve

By the early nineteenth century, naturalists had amassed thousands of specimens from around the world. A pattern kept emerging: species in different parts of the world resembled each other in striking ways, yet were clearly distinct. Island species looked like mainland relatives but showed adaptations to local conditions. The fossil record showed species that no longer existed alongside forms that clearly gave rise to living ones. Something was driving this diversity — but what?

Charles Darwin (1809–1882) and Alfred Russel Wallace (1823–1913) independently arrived at the same answer: natural selection. Darwin had developed his ideas through years of observation, most famously during his voyage on the Beagle (1831–1836) and subsequent study of specimens. Wallace reached similar conclusions through fieldwork in South America and Southeast Asia. The two presented their ideas jointly to the Linnean Society in 1858; Darwin published On the Origin of Species in 1859.

Key Fact

Natural selection requires: (1) variation within a population, (2) some of that variation is heritable (passed to offspring), (3) a selection pressure (environmental challenge), (4) individuals with advantageous variations survive and reproduce more than others — passing those variations on.

The Mechanism of Natural Selection

Variation exists in every natural population. Some of this variation is heritable — it is encoded in the organism’s DNA and can be passed to offspring. Other variation arises from the environment (for example, a plant grown in shade is shorter than a genetically identical plant grown in full light) and is not passed on.

When a selection pressure is applied — a predator, a pathogen, a change in food availability, a change in climate — individuals whose heritable variation best suits them to the new conditions are more likely to survive and reproduce. Their offspring inherit the advantageous variation. Over many generations, this variant becomes more common in the population. Darwin called this process natural selection; the informal summary is “survival of the fittest,” where “fittest” means best adapted to the environment, not strongest or largest.

Antibiotic resistance in bacteria is natural selection in action, occurring rapidly because bacteria reproduce in minutes rather than years. Consider a bacterial population in which rare random mutations have given a tiny fraction of cells resistance to an antibiotic. Most of the population is susceptible. When antibiotic treatment begins, susceptible bacteria die; resistant bacteria survive and reproduce. The next generation is almost entirely resistant. Repeated antibiotic exposure over time can produce strains resistant to multiple drugs.

This is why doctors advise completing a full course of antibiotics: stopping early leaves some susceptible bacteria alive, which then recover and multiply. It also explains why antibiotics should only be prescribed when truly necessary — every unnecessary use is a selection pressure that can drive resistance.

Evidence for Evolution

Darwin’s explanation was compelling because it accounted for multiple independent lines of evidence. Today, the evidence is stronger than it was in 1859 — in part because molecular biology and genetics have provided powerful new tools. The convergence of evidence from completely different scientific fields greatly strengthens confidence in evolutionary theory as an explanation for the diversity of life.

The fossil record — fossils show the preserved remains of organisms in rock strata. Older strata contain simpler organisms; younger strata show progressively more complex and diverse forms. Transitional fossils show organisms with features intermediate between ancestral and descendant groups, exactly as natural selection predicts.

Comparative anatomy — species that share a common ancestor have inherited similar underlying body structures, even when those structures are used for very different purposes. The forelimb bones of a human arm, a whale’s flipper, a bat’s wing, and a horse’s leg all share the same set of bones arranged in the same pattern. This suggests a shared ancestor with that body plan.

DNA comparisons — species with a more recent common ancestor share a greater proportion of their DNA sequence. The most closely related species have the most similar DNA. This molecular evidence is independent of anatomical evidence but reaches the same conclusions about which species are closely related, which strongly supports the common ancestry predicted by natural selection theory.

Speciation

Over very long timescales, natural selection can produce new species. Speciation typically begins with a population being split by a geographical barrier — a mountain range, a river, an ocean. The two isolated groups can no longer interbreed. Each group then experiences different selection pressures — different predators, different food sources, different climates. Over many generations, natural selection produces adaptations suited to each group’s environment. Genetic differences accumulate. Eventually, the two groups become so genetically different that, even if brought back together, they can no longer interbreed and produce fertile offspring. At that point, two species exist where once there was one.

Darwin’s observations of finches on the Galápagos Islands illustrate this process. Different islands had different food sources: seeds, cacti, insects. Populations adapted to local conditions, with beak shape diverging markedly across islands. The different populations descended from a common ancestor but had undergone speciation through geographic isolation and differential selection.

Key Fact

Speciation occurs when geographic isolation separates populations, preventing interbreeding. Different selection pressures in each location drive divergence. Over many generations, genetic differences accumulate until the two populations can no longer interbreed — they are now separate species.

Ideas about Science: How Darwin’s Theory Developed

Darwin’s theory is an excellent example of how scientific explanations develop — and how they differ from simple observation. Before Darwin, the prevailing explanation for species diversity was that each species had been separately created. Darwin and Wallace’s contribution was not just to gather more observations, but to propose a mechanism — natural selection — that could account for all the observations already known.

A good scientific explanation does more than fit the existing data; it makes predictions about what else should be true if the explanation is correct. Natural selection predicts that fossils should show simpler organisms in older strata; that closely related species should share anatomical structures; that DNA sequences should be more similar between closely related species. Each of these predictions has been confirmed independently. The accumulation of evidence from multiple independent fields — geology, anatomy, genetics, ecology — is far more compelling than any single piece of evidence could be on its own.

Darwin did not know about DNA or genes — Gregor Mendel’s work on inheritance (mid-1850s to early 1860s) was largely unknown to the wider scientific community in Darwin’s lifetime. The modern synthesis, which united Darwinian selection with genetics in the twentieth century, strengthened the theory further by providing a molecular explanation for how variation arises (through mutation) and how it is inherited.
lessons.exam_tip_html: Extended-response questions on evolution often reward students who describe the mechanism step by step rather than using vague phrases like “survival of the fittest.” Use precise terms: variation, heritable, selection pressure, differential survival and reproduction, change in allele frequency over generations. For IaS questions asking how Darwin’s theory fits the evidence, explain that convergent evidence from independent fields (fossils, DNA, anatomy) is much stronger than a single source — this is the scientific reasoning the mark scheme rewards.
lessons.conclusion_html:
Key Takeaways

  • Natural selection requires heritable variation, a selection pressure, and differential survival and reproduction — individuals with advantageous variations leave more offspring, shifting the population over generations.
  • Evidence from the fossil record, comparative anatomy and DNA sequencing independently supports common ancestry and evolutionary change; convergent evidence from multiple fields greatly strengthens the theory.
  • Speciation occurs when geographic isolation prevents interbreeding, allowing different selection pressures to drive divergence until two populations can no longer produce fertile offspring together.

lessons.title: Biodiversity and Classification
lessons.description: Why diversity matters and how scientists group the living world.
lessons.content_html:
What is Biodiversity?

Biodiversity is the variety of species found in a given area. High biodiversity makes ecosystems more stable and resilient — if one species declines, others can take over its ecological role. Low biodiversity makes an ecosystem fragile and more likely to collapse when conditions change.

Key Fact

High biodiversity increases ecosystem resilience. A diverse community has more species to fill each ecological role, so the system can absorb disturbances without collapsing. Coral reefs and tropical rainforests are two of the most biodiverse — and most threatened — ecosystems on Earth.

Threats to Biodiversity

Human activities are the main driver of biodiversity loss worldwide. Key threats include:

  • Deforestation — clearing forests for agriculture, timber or development destroys habitats and the species within them. Tropical deforestation is particularly damaging because rainforests hold an exceptionally large proportion of the world’s species.
  • Habitat destruction — converting land to farmland, draining wetlands and building on greenfield sites all reduce the area available for wild species.
  • Climate change — rising temperatures shift the ranges where species can survive. Coral bleaching, caused by warmer sea temperatures, is a clear example: when sea temperatures rise above a threshold, coral reefs expel the algae they depend on, turning white and dying.
  • Pollution — pesticides, fertiliser runoff, plastic waste and air pollution all harm organisms. Fertiliser runoff triggers eutrophication in freshwater, causing oxygen depletion and mass die-offs.
  • Overexploitation — overfishing, illegal hunting and unsustainable harvesting reduce populations below sustainable levels.

UK wild bee and hoverfly populations have declined significantly in recent decades. Intensification of farming — which reduces wildflower meadows and hedgerows — is a major driver, alongside pesticide use and habitat fragmentation. Pollinators matter far beyond their own survival: roughly three-quarters of flowering plant species depend on animal pollinators to reproduce. A collapse in pollinator diversity would cascade through food chains, threatening crop yields and wild plant communities alike.

This case illustrates a key principle: biodiversity loss is rarely isolated. Losing one group of species weakens the ecological services that other species — including humans — depend on. Scientists describe this as the loss of ecosystem services.

Conservation Strategies

Scientists and governments use a range of strategies to protect biodiversity:

  • Protected areas — national parks, nature reserves and Sites of Special Scientific Interest (SSSIs) restrict damaging human activity within ecologically important habitats.
  • Captive breeding programmes — zoos and wildlife centres breed endangered species with the aim of reintroducing them into the wild when conditions are safe.
  • Seed banks — repositories such as the Svalbard Global Seed Vault preserve plant genetic diversity, safeguarding against extinction.
  • Legislation — international agreements and national laws restrict hunting and trade of threatened species, and regulate pollution.
  • Habitat restoration — planting hedgerows, restoring wetlands and creating wildlife corridors help fragmented populations reconnect.

Classification: Grouping the Living World

Classification is the process of grouping organisms based on shared features. The modern system was developed by the Swedish scientist Carl Linnaeus (1707–1778), who introduced a hierarchy of groups and a formal naming system.

Key Fact

The classification hierarchy from most inclusive to least is: Kingdom → Phylum → Class → Order → Family → Genus → Species. A useful mnemonic is: King Philip Came Over For Good Soup. Members of the same species can interbreed and produce fertile offspring.

The Binomial Naming System

Every species is given a unique two-part Latin name — this is the binomial system. The first part is the genus name (always capitalised) and the second is the species name (always lowercase). For example, modern humans are Homo sapiens and the domestic dog is Canis lupus familiaris. Using Latin ensures scientists worldwide share the same name for each species, avoiding confusion caused by different common names in different languages.

The Five Kingdoms

Organisms are traditionally divided into five kingdoms:

  • Animals — multicellular, heterotrophic (cannot make their own food), no cell wall.
  • Plants — multicellular, autotrophic (photosynthesise), cellulose cell wall.
  • Fungi — multicellular (mostly), heterotrophic, chitin cell wall, reproduce by spores.
  • Protists — mostly unicellular eukaryotes that do not fit the other kingdoms (e.g. Amoeba, algae).
  • Prokaryotes (Bacteria) — unicellular, no nucleus, no membrane-bound organelles.

Classification is more than a filing system — it reflects evolutionary history. Species that are closely related share a more recent common ancestor and tend to share more DNA sequences. Modern genomic techniques allow scientists to compare the DNA of different organisms directly, refining classifications that were previously based only on visible (morphological) features. This is an example of a scientific model being updated as new evidence becomes available — early classifications based purely on appearance sometimes grouped unrelated organisms together just because they looked alike (convergent evolution).

For instance, dolphins were historically mistaken for fish because of their body shape. DNA evidence places them firmly within mammals, closely related to even-toed ungulates (cattle, pigs and deer). This illustrates why multiple lines of evidence — morphology, biochemistry and DNA — are all considered in modern classification.
lessons.exam_tip_html: For ‘Evaluate’ questions on conservation, always weigh both practical and ethical dimensions — examiners want to see reasoned judgement, not just a list of strategies. When writing the binomial name in an answer, remember: genus is capitalised, species is lowercase, and the whole name is italicised (underlined in handwriting). On ‘Explain why biodiversity matters’ questions, link biodiversity to ecosystem stability and to specific services humans rely on, such as pollination and food production — a vague “it’s good for nature” will not score full marks.
lessons.conclusion_html:
Key Takeaways

  • Biodiversity — the variety of species in an ecosystem — is being reduced by deforestation, climate change, pollution and overexploitation. High biodiversity underpins resilient ecosystems and the services they provide to humans.
  • Conservation strategies include protected areas, captive breeding, seed banks, habitat restoration and legislation. Each addresses a different threat but all share the goal of preventing irreversible species loss.
  • Classification groups organisms into a hierarchy (kingdom to species) using shared features and evolutionary relationships. The binomial system gives every species a unique Latin name: genus (capital) followed by species (lowercase), written in italics.

practice_questions.marks:
Mastering:
For: Loss of species is irreversible; biodiversity supports ecosystem services (pollination, clean water, food); high-biodiversity ecosystems are more resilient to climate change; future species may have medical or scientific value not yet discovered [up to 3 marks for developed points].
Against: Economic development lifts communities out of poverty; sustainable land use can coexist with biodiversity; blanket protection may be seen as imposing costs on developing nations [up to 2 marks].
Conclusion: Justified conclusion that weighs the evidence — e.g. biodiversity loss is largely irreversible whereas economic damage can be recovered, suggesting biodiversity protection should have priority where trade-offs must be made [1 mark].
Secure: Both sides addressed, conclusion present but less developed.
Developing: One side only, limited development.
Emerging: Simple assertion without evidence.

glossary_terms.definition: The variety of all the different species of organisms on Earth, or within a particular ecosystem.
Reef structures built by colonies of coral polyps. Coral bleaching occurs when warmer water stresses the corals, causing them to expel their photosynthetic algae and turn white.
The rapid growth of algae in water caused by excess nutrients, which reduces oxygen levels and kills other aquatic organisms.
The benefits that functioning ecosystems provide to humans, including food production, clean water, pollination, climate regulation and recreation.
The systematic grouping of organisms into hierarchical categories based on shared characteristics and evolutionary relationships.
A two-part scientific naming system for species, consisting of the genus name (capitalised) followed by the species name (lowercase), written in italics.
The broadest level of biological classification, grouping all organisms into five major categories: animals, plants, fungi, protists and prokaryotes (bacteria).
